Church, Crown and Civil Authority

The royal council has received rival proposals for religious government. One would restore an inquisitorial tribunal and empower clergy in colonial administration. Opponents warn that coercive jurisdiction would deepen local resistance and estrange foreign courts. The other proposal maintains a privileged Church under ordinary royal law.
Restore the Holy Office under royal authority.
Keep ecclesiastical matters under ordinary law.
Set the African Expedition Accounts
Create an audited fund for charts, supplies and the fleet. This is preparation for a possible campaign, not a declaration of war.
Provision the Strait Depots
Stock the Spanish shore with naval stores and establish a supply office for the Moroccan coast. The court still has to authorize a campaign.
Authorize the Campaign for Tangier
Declare war on Morocco with Tangier as the stated territorial demand. Morocco retains its land unless the demand is secured in a peace settlement.
The Tangier Settlement

The kingdom holds Tangier after a peace with Morocco. The cabinet must choose how to govern the new coast. Communities, religious authorities and merchants will judge the new administration by its conduct.
Convene local councils and a civil administration.
Place the coast under military and clerical authority.
The Moroccan Campaign Ends
The war has ended without a Spanish settlement in Tangier. The ministry closes the expedition accounts and confronts the political cost of failure.
Receive the campaign report.
Establish the Moroccan Mission Courts

The Holy Office proposes new tribunals and schools in the Spanish-held coast. Its reach depends on actual Spanish administration. Local residents will resist coercive rule, and neighboring states will scrutinize it.
Fund Schools on the Moroccan Coast
Support teachers, interpreters and municipal offices in Spanish-held Moroccan districts. The programme works gradually and cannot itself claim new land.
Press the Moroccan Interior
Authorize a new war for the Marrakesh state. This larger campaign requires the Tangier coast and must still be won through a peace settlement.
Administration Beyond the Coast
The kingdom now holds Marrakesh after a separate settlement. A wider occupation requires roads, civil offices and a continuing response to local opposition.
Open a provincial administration.
The Inland Campaign Ends
The war has ended without the inland territorial settlement. The court must account for the expedition before considering new demands.
Close the expedition account.
The Limits of the African Crown

Spanish ministers have proposed a wider Maghreb dominion. French and British interests, Moroccan sovereignty and the costs of governing the occupied districts now place limits on that ambition. The royal council can consolidate its actual holdings or seek further claims through ordinary diplomacy and war.
Consolidate the territory we actually govern.
Issue a Philippine Royal Charter
Establish a royal council for the Philippine provinces, with representation from local municipalities and the existing Spanish and Filipino communities. The charter funds administration

column2: Schools and Teachers in Manila

Fund the schools and teacher colleges.

Recognize the Hispano-Filipino Councils

After the charter and school programme, crown officials can recognize the Hispano-Filipino communities already represented in the islands. Their accepted status opens offices and civic institutions, while other grievances and independence movements can still arise.
The Philippine Reform Movement

Writers and municipal leaders are demanding representation and legal reform. The royal charter gives them an institutional route, but the government must decide whether to hear their petitions. This does not prevent later nationalist organizing.
Hear the petitions in the royal council.
Suppress the petition campaign.

The Moroccan Littoral and Its Authorities

The Sultan's appointed qaids, port merchants and local Rif leaders do not speak with one voice. A Spanish foothold can be supplied through recognized officials and negotiated contracts, through private coastal brokers, or by funding rivals against the Moroccan court. Each choice changes the trust the crown can expect beyond its walls.
